A neural network computes its output with many simple units, the neurons, each of which forms a weighted sum of its inputs and passes it through a nonlinear function. This section follows the idea from its beginnings to the multilayer network. We start with a short history, because the setbacks of the field explain many design decisions of today’s networks. Then we look at the perceptron, the first trainable neuron, and at the reason why one layer of perceptrons is not enough. The section ends with the multilayer network and a small example network that
Three Waves of Neural Network Research

children.label: Three Waves of Neural Network Research

children.value: shows the milestones of the first decades. The

began with a model of the biological neuron. McCulloch and Pitts described in 1943 a neuron as a threshold unit that fires when the weighted sum of its inputs exceeds a threshold. In 1958, Rosenblatt turned this unit into the

, a neuron that learns its weights from examples, and built it in hardware. Several perceptrons could work in parallel, but each connected the inputs directly to an output. In 1969, Minsky and Papert showed that such a single layer cannot compute even simple functions such as the exclusive or (XOR), which the next subsection explains. Interest in neural networks declined for more than a decade.

children.alt: Milestones of neural network research from 1943 to 2006.

came in the 1980s with networks that have hidden layers between input and output, and with an algorithm to train them. Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams popularized

in 1986; the underlying method of computing derivatives backward through a chain of functions had appeared earlier, in work by Linnainmaa (1970) and Werbos (1974). The revival produced convolutional networks, recurrent networks, and belief networks, many of the concepts of modern deep learning. Yet deeper networks were unstable and slow to train, for reasons that

explains, and computers were too slow for large networks. From the early 1990s until the early 2010s, support vector machines with well-chosen kernels matched or beat neural networks on most benchmarks.

Convolutional networks existed long before they won. LeNet read handwritten digits in the 1990s, but for almost two decades it was not clear whether convolutional networks would scale from small digit images to large collections of realistic photos. Early networks also depended on many hand-designed steps and solved one task only, as the face detector in
trains small fully connected networks in the browser and makes the limits of the early multilayer networks tangible.

started in the mid-2000s. A research program of the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research, led by Hinton, kept the field alive when funding was scarce. In 2006, Hinton, Osindero, and Teh showed how to train deep belief networks layer by layer, and the field adopted the name
. At the same time, graphics processors became fast and programmable. They compute the matrix products of a network in parallel and trained networks in days instead of weeks.

shows how the energy efficiency of these processors grew over the following decade. In 2012, a network trained by the Google Brain project on 16,000 processor cores learned to detect cats in YouTube frames without any labels. In the same year, AlexNet won the ImageNet challenge with a large margin and showed for the first time that features learned from data beat features designed by hand on a large benchmark.

The rule does not minimize an objective function. It is a heuristic that stops as soon as all examples are classified correctly. If a separating hyperplane exists, that is, if the data is

, the rule finds one after a finite number of corrections. It finds one of many possible hyperplanes, and which one depends on the order of the examples. If no separating hyperplane exists, the rule never stops correcting.
The exclusive or is the classic counterexample. XOR outputs 1 for

children.value: . No line separates the two pairs, because the points of each pair lie on opposite corners of the unit square. A single perceptron therefore cannot compute XOR, and neither can any single layer of perceptrons, since each output is a perceptron of its own.

compares the perceptron with the support vector machine on a separable problem. The perceptron accepts any separating line, while the support vector machine chooses the one with the largest distance to the nearest examples of both classes.

How powerful are such networks? The

states that a network with a single hidden layer and enough neurons can approximate any continuous function on a bounded region as closely as desired (Cybenko 1989, Hornik 1991). The theorem says nothing about how many neurons are needed or how to find their weights. In practice, deep networks with many smaller layers learn more efficiently than shallow networks with one huge layer, because each layer can build on the representation of the previous one.
